practice1.prompt: write the tests for apply_discount before the function exists

cases.name: your tests pass the working version and catch all three bugs
cases.reference:
def apply_discount(price, percent):
    return price - price * percent / 100

practice1.hint: The starter test uses a price of 100 and a discount of 20, and every one of the three broken versions survives it -- 100 minus 20 is 80 either way. Change the numbers so the percentage and the amount are not the same, then add the two cases the lesson points at: a discount of nothing, and a price that does not divide evenly.

questions.prompt: Put the test-driven development cycle in order.
items: Write just enough code to make it pass
Tidy the code up without changing what it does
questions.explain: Red, green, refactor. The test comes first so that it is seen to fail for the right reason before any code exists to make it pass.

questions.prompt: Why does the cycle start with a test that fails?
choices: To make sure the test can fail at all
To make the suite run faster
So the code can be written afterwards in any order
questions.explain: A test written after the code and never seen red might be passing for a reason that has nothing to do with the code. Watching it fail first proves it is connected to the thing it claims to check.

questions.prompt: Which decisions did writing the discount tests first force you to make?
choices: What a discount of zero percent should return
Whether percent means a percentage or an amount off
questions.explain: Each of the three is a decision that would otherwise have been settled by accident, by whichever line of code happened to get typed first.

questions.prompt: You write a test, and it passes immediately without any new code. What does that mean?
choices: Something is wrong: either the test does not check what you meant, or the behaviour already existed
questions.explain: A green test at the Red step is a warning, not a shortcut. Usually the assertion is not reaching the code it was aimed at.
